sources.title: Zipf's Law and Cache Hit Ratios: Why Your Caching Math Fails When ...
sources.snippet: If you assume a strict Zipfian distribution, the relationship between cache size and hit rate is non-linear. The first few gigabytes of cache yield massive rewards, but you quickly hit a point of diminishing returns where adding more memory barely moves the needle.

sources.title: Caching — Hit Rates, Zipf and the Working Set · nonconvexcard
sources.snippet: Caching feels like it should have a threshold: store enough and everything hits. Under realistic popularity it does not. Request popularity is heavily skewed but has a long tail, and the consequence is that hit rate grows like a power of cache size — you buy a fixed multiplicative improvement per order of magnitude of memory, forever, without ever arriving.

sources.title: Lower Bounds for Caching with Delayed Hits
sources.snippet: Caches are a fundamental component of latency-sensitive computer systems. Recent work of [ASWB20] has initiated the study of delayed hits: a phenomenon in caches that occurs when the latency between the cache and backing store is much larger than the time between new requests. We present two results for the delayed hits caching model. (1) Competitive ratio lower bound.
